## What Part Two Is

Part Two of *Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research with R*
is about latent-variable modeling. The methods of Part One worked with
variables that were recorded: a test score, a count, a group label. Here the
variable of primary interest is one that no column of the data set holds.
Twelve questionnaire items are recorded; the planning, the learning
strategies and the sense of belonging those items are meant to register are
not. Part Two asks what follows from taking that situation seriously, and
answers through factor analysis: how observed responses represent latent
variables, and how a measurement model is developed, specified, estimated,
evaluated and extended.

It is written for postgraduate students and applied researchers who have read
Part One or who already command the statistics it develops: variable form,
variance, covariance and correlation; estimates, sampling uncertainty,
intervals and tests, with the limits of a dichotomous decision; regression
equations, residuals and conditional comparisons; nested model comparison and
penalized in-sample criteria; held-out evidence; and reproducible work in R.
Part One's argument-based reading of a study is useful background rather than
a prerequisite. One optional section of Chapter 1 applies it to the
latent-variable case, and nothing later depends on it.

Four chapters form the measurement sequence, and this introduction is about
them. Chapter 1, *From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis*, is the
general and conceptual presentation. Chapter 2, *Exploratory Factor Analysis
and Model Development*, is the exploratory approach, conceptual and
practical. Chapter 3, *Specifying and Estimating Confirmatory Factor Models*,
is the foundational confirmatory approach, covering concepts, specification
and estimation. Chapter 4, *Evaluating and Comparing Confirmatory Factor
Models*, is the advanced confirmatory approach, covering evaluation,
comparison and the higher-order and bifactor extensions. The chapters after
them carry the structural half of the subject, from relations between factors
and indicators to relations among variables in a structural system; the last
section here says what they cover and what they cannot confer.

Part Two asks for more mathematics than Part One did. Readers manipulate
equations, count the moments a covariance matrix supplies against the
parameters a model spends, and work with small vectors and matrices: a matrix
product, a transpose, a symmetric matrix, a diagonal matrix. No previous
course in factor algebra or matrix calculus is assumed. Each new operation
appears first in a scalar or two-variable case, substantive and graphical
meaning comes before notation, and every symbol, index and dimension is
defined before it is used. Calculus and proof-based mathematical statistics
are not prerequisites, and long proofs, general identification theorems,
extended matrix derivations, asymptotic distribution theory and hand
optimization are placed so that a reader can pass over them without losing a
definition, an equation or an assumption the main route needs.

The book chapters carry the statistics. A model appears as equations, as
parameter matrices, as a path diagram and as an explanation; every reported
number is computed for the reader and read in prose and in named tables, and
no chapter displays R code. The software that specifies, fits and extracts
each model belongs to the Computer Lab beside the chapter, where every model
a chapter reports has a task that fits it. A reader who never opens R can
still follow every model, every count and every conclusion from the printed
evidence. Readers who meet these chapters in a course may also receive
companion materials -- lecture notes, exercise handouts, homework, and
Computer Labs with worked answers -- but the chapters stand on their own.

Each chapter opens in the same way. A **Chapter overview** box summarizes the
whole chapter in ordinary words: the route, and what a reader will be able to
do at the end. The prose that follows it begins from a real measurement
problem or concern in an applied study and states the question the chapter
answers. Each chapter closes with a numbered **Summary and reading bridge**
that gathers what has been settled and states the questions the next chapter
owes. A short **Key terms** table follows where a chapter carries one, then answer-free exercises, then any appendices, which hold derivations, data documentation and extensions the main route does not require.

## The Measurement Problem at a Glance

Several recorded responses vary together, and the attribute used to explain
their association is not recorded at all. The common-factor model proposes an
account of that covariation: each recorded response is written as a common
part, shared with the other responses through a small number of unobserved
variables, plus a residual part that the declared common variables do not
represent. That sentence is the model. The algebra makes it precise and gives
it consequences that data can contradict.

For $p$ indicators and $m$ factors, with $\mathbf y_i$ the $p\times1$ vector
of responses recorded for unit $i$,

$$
\mathbf y_i=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta_i
  +\boldsymbol\epsilon_i,
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)
  &=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\alpha,\\
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)
  &=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi
    \boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Theta,
\end{aligned}
$$

with $E(\boldsymbol\epsilon_i)=\mathbf 0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\eta_i,\boldsymbol\epsilon_i)=\mathbf 0$. Here
$\boldsymbol\nu$ holds the $p$ indicator intercepts, $\boldsymbol\eta_i$ the
$m$ factors for unit $i$, $\boldsymbol\Lambda$ the $p\times m$ loadings that
relate the two, and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_i$ the $p$ residuals;
$\boldsymbol\alpha$ holds the $m$ latent intercepts, $\boldsymbol\Phi$ is the
$m\times m$ factor covariance matrix, $\boldsymbol\Theta$ the $p\times p$
residual covariance matrix, and $\boldsymbol\vartheta$ the complete vector of
free parameters. What the model produces is the implied pair: a mean
structure $\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)$ and a covariance structure
$\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)$. An analysis working from
covariances alone sets the mean structure aside or profiles it out under
stated assumptions, which is a choice rather than an absence. One notation
serves all four chapters, and it is chosen to survive the move to structural
models, so that later chapters extend the model rather than quietly changing
what its symbols mean.

The covariance equation is what makes the proposal answerable. Declared
loadings, factor relations and residual restrictions imply one particular
covariance matrix, and that matrix can be held against the one a sample
supplies. The comparison has force because a covariance matrix for $p$
indicators holds only $p(p+1)/2$ distinct entries: a model that spends fewer
parameters than that makes claims which can fail. Counting the information
indicators supply against the parameters a model spends is a recurring
operation in Part Two, and it is kept separate from the further question of
whether those moments determine the parameters at all.

None of this makes a factor identical to the construct that names it. A
**construct** is a substantive idea belonging to the research question, and
its meaning comes from theory, item content, response processes, the
population studied and the use intended for the results, none of which a
covariance matrix supplies. A **factor** is a random variable inside a
statistical model, and an observed or estimated **score** is neither; the
three are never treated as synonyms. The arrow a path diagram draws from a
factor to an indicator states the direction of representation the model
adopts, writing each response as a function of the factors plus a residual.
It is not a finding that the factor produces the response, and it is the
wrong direction for a construct whose indicators produce it. Fit to
covariance evidence becomes construct and score language only when item
content, response processes, population and intended use also support that
reading.

Part Two models continuous indicators and continuous outcomes. Ordered
categorical indicators, thresholds, polychoric correlations, ordered-response
factor models and their estimator-specific conventions are signposted where a
reader would meet them and are taught elsewhere; numeric category codes are
not automatically continuous measurements. The boundary concerns the
indicators rather than every variable in a study. Categorical grouping
variables and dummy-coded predictors stay in scope, and the later multigroup
and MIMIC work uses them alongside continuous indicators. Full-information
maximum likelihood for missing continuous responses and robust maximum
likelihood for inference under nonnormality are later topics as well, and
neither is a switch to categorical measurement.

The model family is the reflective common-factor measurement model with its
higher-order and bifactor relatives, estimated by normal-theory maximum
likelihood as one coherent lineage across exploratory and confirmatory work;
principal components analysis answers a different question and is not a
common-factor estimator. What the family cannot do is as settled as what it
can. No factor analysis establishes that a latent entity exists, that a
reflective direction is causal, that a scale is valid, or that a structural
claim is warranted. Higher-order and bifactor models are rival
representations of an adequate core model rather than repairs for a weak one,
and reliability follows a defined score, model, population and use: it is not
validity, and it does not mend a weak measurement representation.

## How Chapters 1--4 Progress

The four chapters make four connected moves on one covariance equation:
**represent** a common-factor model and derive the moments it implies;
**explore** a development record to settle dimensionality, orientation and
interpretation; **specify and estimate** the resulting proposal as explicit
restrictions on evidence that played no part in producing it; and
**evaluate, compare and extend** the fitted model. The equation is the same
throughout. What changes at each stage is the responsibility it carries and
the evidence it must answer to. @fig-part-two-route sets out that
architecture; no chapter redraws it.

The stopping points are as deliberate as the moves. Chapter 2 does not
relabel a developed pattern as confirmation. Chapter 3 does not treat
convergence or admissibility as adequate fit, and says so in its own section
title: it reads an estimated model *before its fit*. Chapter 4 does not treat
favorable fit as construct validation. Each chapter completes one
responsibility and transfers a defined record, rather than carrying an
unexamined conclusion forward under a new name.

## Evidence Roles Across the Sequence

Using one model family repeatedly does not give every record the same
inferential role. Part Two keeps the analysis history visible so that
development, first evaluation and independent revalidation are not collapsed
into one favorable account. Every decision is developmental, planned in
advance, a planned sensitivity, or post hoc, always in relation to a named
body of evidence, and that status follows the timing and provenance of the
decision rather than the name of the function that fitted it: a model
developed after inspecting a record is exploratory with respect to that
record whatever routine estimates it. @tbl-part-two-evidence gives the
principal roles.

| Record | First permitted use | What it cannot establish by itself |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Known-value six-indicator records** | Chapter 1 reconstructs an implied covariance matrix entrywise from parameters declared in advance | Sampling behavior, an empirical factor count, a unique rotation, a best model, or the existence of the constructs the columns are named after |
| **SLE Sample A, 360 cases, development** | Chapter 2 audits the indicators, develops the exploratory solution, and freezes the candidate with its named rivals | Independent confirmation of any choice made while Sample A was being inspected |
| **SLE Sample B, 360 cases, confirmation** | Chapter 3 estimates the frozen candidate; Chapter 4 evaluates it, diagnoses it, and compares the rivals declared in advance | Independent support for a relation first noticed in Sample B, which stays exploratory until fresh evidence tests it |
| **SLE Sample C, 360 cases, revalidation** | Chapter 4 evaluates the one revision frozen after Sample B | General validity, measurement invariance, or permission to search Sample C repeatedly for a revision that survives |
| **Known SLE generating moments** | Chapter 4 discloses them only after the Sample B and Sample C sequence is complete, then computes the population optimum and the population discrepancies directly | Contemporaneous justification for an earlier choice, or a finite-sample conclusion from one realization beyond what the audit separates |
| **Separate donor microcases** | Compact demonstrations of a specified calculation or model comparison, declared from their own population and seed | The development or confirmation status of the SLE sequence, which they never join |

The Student Learning Experiences (SLE) records are a synthetic course case:
continuous simulated data, not observations from actual students and not a
validated instrument. Three independent samples of 360 complete cases carry
twelve indicators -- four Planning, four Strategy and four Belonging -- drawn
from one declared population and distributed together in
`sle_continuous.csv` beside the chapters. Each analysis uses only the sample
its role entitles it to, and Chapter 1 uses none of them; the Chapter 2
appendix supplies the codebook, the sample manifest and the generating
population, so that every reported value can be reproduced. The samples are
never pooled to manufacture a larger analysis, availability is not permission
to use a record early, and a record that becomes exploratory through revision
does not recover confirmatory status because the next command is named after
confirmation.

The retrospective audit that closes Chapter 4 follows the same discipline in
reverse. It is possible only because the population is known, and it is
disclosed only after the Sample B and Sample C sequence has run its course:
first the evidence a researcher could actually have had, then the generating
structure the candidate omitted. The audit adds no further sample, no new
candidate and no successful revision, and it supplies no after-the-fact
justification for a choice made earlier. Its value is that a reader watches a
model stay coherent, reproducible and apparently well fitting while still
owing a narrower conclusion than its name suggests -- which no real study can
show.

## Boundaries and What Follows

The chapters after Chapter 4 continue Part Two from relations between factors
and indicators to relations among variables in a structural system. Their
subject is observed-variable path analysis; general structural equation
modeling; measurement invariance and multigroup measurement; MIMIC models;
latent regression and indirect effects; latent growth in a structural
equation form; and structural model comparison, ordered by their research
questions rather than by a software menu. Multilevel modeling, including
multilevel growth, belongs to Part Three -- a division of the curriculum, not
a claim that structural and multilevel parameterizations stop being
equivalent when observations are unbalanced or incomplete. Item-response
theory, mixture models, multilevel factor analysis and a full treatment of
categorical indicators lie outside Part Two altogether.

The measurement sequence ends where a reader can read and evaluate a
measurement representation, and structural work begins where a new question
requires relations among variables or among factors. An acceptable
measurement model is necessary evidence for many latent-variable structural
analyses, but a measurement portion plus a structural portion confers no
substantive warrant: structural equation modeling does not upgrade an
associational design to a causal one, does not erase measurement uncertainty,
and does not make an indirect effect causal by calling it mediation. Before
latent means or structural parameters are compared across groups, settings or
occasions, the relevant level of measurement comparability is addressed with
the loading, intercept and other restrictions it requires; and a growth model
addresses both mean trajectories and the variation and covariation in
trajectories. The bridge out of Chapter 4 is written with that in view, so
that a latent intercept is not mistaken for the marginal latent mean once
structural regressions enter.

Part One's argument vocabulary is reused rather than redefined, and Part Two
does not re-teach the argument-based approach as a recurring apparatus. One
optional section of Chapter 1 shows how evidence, justification,
interpretation and claim boundaries change when a statistical variable is
latent, applies the six quality-evaluation questions under Part One's names,
records at least one failed verdict and repairs the claim. A reader may skip
it without losing a definition, an equation, an exercise or a prerequisite
for the chapters that follow, and Chapters 2 to 4 express prespecification,
analytic status, uncertainty, limitations and claim boundaries in the
ordinary technical vocabulary of exploratory and confirmatory factor
analysis.

The software is allocated as deliberately as the evidence. Chapter 1's
chapter text needs no student software: its records are constructed, its
results exact, and its conclusions readable without a computer. The Computer
Labs install the small pinned stack once, before it is needed, and then put
it to work where the statistics require it -- `psych` and `GPArotation` for
the exploratory work from Chapter 2, and `lavaan` for the confirmatory fits
from Chapter 3. A chapter names the software it relies on and states the
consequential defaults in words -- scale setting, factor covariances, mean
structures, missing-data handling, standard errors and the test-statistic
family -- while the commands themselves stay in the labs.

The reference that follows is the single vocabulary for the four chapters. Its
four concept tables gather related terms into broad concept groups and give
each term's meaning or essential distinction; a closing table records the
notation the chapters use. In the concept tables the **Main explanation**
column is a destination, the chapter and section where the term is principally

table the **Main use** column carries that destination and a final column

meanings have separate entries, and a symbol whose preferred form carries a
qualifier takes a row of its own that names its other uses. First-use
explanations, worked examples and the reasons behind each distinction stay in

| Covariance structure | Pattern matrix and structure matrix ($\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$) | $\boldsymbol\Lambda$ holds the coefficients of the indicator equations; $\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$ holds indicator-factor covariances. They coincide under orthogonal unit-variance factors and must be read side by side in an oblique solution. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5; oblique reading Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 |
| Covariance structure | Communality ($h_j^{2}$) | The common part of an indicator's variance, $\boldsymbol\lambda_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\lambda_j$, under the declared model. The shortcut $\lambda_j^{2}$ holds only for one nonzero loading on a unit-variance factor; correlated factors add a cross term. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1 |
| Covariance structure | Uniqueness (residual variance; Heywood case) | $\theta_{jj}=1-h_j^{2}$ for a standardized indicator: variance the declared common factors do not represent, which is not the same as random error. A negative estimate is an improper, or Heywood, solution. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1 |
| Covariance structure | Moment structure ($\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)$) | The modeled object is the mean and covariance pair; $\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\alpha$. Analysing covariances alone sets the mean structure aside, which is a choice rather than an absence. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.2 |
| Covariance structure | Distinct moment and degrees of freedom ($u=p(p+1)/2$, $df=u-t$) | The number of distinct entries a covariance matrix supplies, and its difference from the free-parameter count. More respondents estimate the same moments more precisely; $df\ge0$ is necessary for, and never proof of, identification. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.3 |
| Covariance structure | Tetrad restriction | The vanishing of $\sigma_{jk}\sigma_{lm}-\sigma_{jm}\sigma_{lk}$, which one common factor with uncorrelated residuals forces for every four indicators. A nonzero tetrad refutes exact reproduction by that model, whatever its loadings. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.3 |
| Covariance structure | SS loading (column sum of squared loadings) | A summary of one factor column across indicators, read after rotation as a column statistic of the oriented solution. It is not in general an eigenvalue of the analysed correlation matrix, the matrix being decomposed must always be named, and with correlated factors it gives no unique additive partition of common variance. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.1; post-rotation reading Chapter 2, Sec. 3.2 |
| Neighboring objects | Factor-score estimate ($\widehat{\eta}_{ik}$) | A prediction of an unobserved factor value from responses, a fitted model and a scoring rule. Different rules give different numbers from the same fit, and no rule makes it an error-free measurement. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5 |
| Neighboring objects | Principal component and prespecified composite | Weighted composites of observed variables, one chosen to capture observed variance and one declared as a rule such as a sum or mean. Neither decomposes covariance into common and residual parts, so neither answers the common-factor model's question. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5 |
| Analytic orientation | Exploratory, confirmatory and hybrid orientation | Names for how much is declared before the focal analysis, not for unrelated models. Both use the same covariance decomposition; the restrictions and the history of the decisions separate them. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.4 and 6.6 |
| Analytic orientation | Analytic status (development versus confirmation evidence) | The record of which body of evidence informed each decision. A specification chosen on one body of evidence receives a genuinely new test only from evidence not used to choose it; analyses move from confirmatory to exploratory status and never back. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.6--6.7 |

### Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development {#sec-p2-concepts-efa .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Exploratory analysis | Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) | A common-factor analysis that leaves most loading restrictions open while seeking a comparatively low-dimensional representation of shared covariation. It is not assumption-free: the indicator set, population, association matrix, residual restriction, dimensional range and rotation criterion all shape what it can reveal. | Chapter 2, Sec. 1 |
| Exploratory analysis | Development sample (development record) | The sample whose inspection produces a model. A model developed after inspecting these observations is exploratory with respect to them whatever fitting function is used, so the same records cannot confirm it. | Chapter 2, Sec. 1 |
| Extraction | Squared multiple correlation (SMC) | For indicator $j$, the $R^2$ from regressing it on all other indicators, computed as $1-1/(\mathbf R^{-1})_{jj}$. It is a regression summary of the observed matrix used as a communality start, not a known common variance. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Reduced correlation matrix (SMC-reduced matrix) | The correlation matrix with communality estimates replacing the unit diagonal. It need not be positive semidefinite, and its eigenvalues are on a different scale from the full matrix's. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Principal-axis factoring (PAF) | Iterative extraction that decomposes a reduced matrix, forms loadings from its leading positive roots and updates the diagonal from row sums of squared loadings. The diagonal start, nonpositive-root handling and stopping rule are implementation choices. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Minimum-residual extraction (minres) | Extraction minimizing the sum of squared off-diagonal correlation residuals, giving each displayed discrepancy equal weight. It is a common-factor method but not another name for PAF. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4 |
| Retention | Kaiser--Guttman rule (eigenvalue-greater-than-one) | Retaining roots above one in a unit-diagonal correlation analysis. Sampling variation alone produces roots above one, and applying the threshold to a reduced matrix changes the comparison. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3 |
| Retention | Scree plot | An ordered plot of eigenvalues read for where large decreases give way to a flatter sequence. It supplies no sampling reference, and full- and reduced-matrix plots need not agree. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3 |
| Retention | Parallel analysis (permutation parallel analysis) | Comparing each observed eigenvalue with the same-rank eigenvalues of datasets built to have no common factors but the same sample size and marginal distributions, and retaining the leading consecutive run that clears its reference. The eigenvalue basis, the null generator, the reference statistic and the replication count and seed all belong to the specification. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.4 |
| Retention | Empirical Kaiser criterion (EKC) | A sample-adjusted repair of Kaiser--Guttman using the Marchenko--Pastur bound $(1+\sqrt{p/n})^2$ for the first root, correcting later roots for variance already accounted for and flooring the reference at one. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Retention | Sequential model tests | Fitting successive factor counts and stopping at the first non-significant exact-fit test. The sequence is trustworthy only while still under-fitting, because the $\chi^2$ reference fails once the count exceeds the true number. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Retention | Combination rule | Using two criteria with different references together, and treating their disagreement as evidence that the dimensions are hard to detect rather than as a tie to be broken by vote. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Counting | Effective EFA parameter count ($t_m$) | $pm+p-m(m-1)/2$ for an unrestricted common-factor covariance model at regular points, with $df_m=p(p+1)/2-t_m$. The subtraction removes rotational redundancy; an oblique rotation adds no parameters because it re-expresses the same fitted covariance. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1 |
| Counting | Ledermann bound | The largest factor count the covariance moments can generically support, $m\le(2p+1-\sqrt{8p+1})/2$. It is a counting limit, not a recommendation, a positive-root count or a proof of identification. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1 |
| Rotation | Inverse-paired transformation | The general nonsingular change of factor coordinates $\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf T^{-1}$ with $\mathbf T\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf T^{\mathsf T}$, which leaves the fitted common covariance unchanged. Multiplying loadings while leaving $\boldsymbol\Phi$ alone is not an equivalent oblique rotation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.1 |
| Rotation | Varimax | An orthogonal criterion maximizing the dispersion of squared loadings within columns. A clean varimax pattern does not establish that the substantive attributes are unrelated. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Rotation | Direct oblimin (quartimin at $\gamma=0$) | An oblique criterion discouraging large squared coefficients in several columns of one row while permitting factor correlations. The name alone is not a specification: $\gamma$, normalization, tolerance, iteration limit, starts and seed all matter. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Rotation | Kaiser normalization | Dividing each loading row by its communality-based length before optimizing and restoring the scale afterward, which reweights indicators in the criterion. It is not the same operation as standardizing the observed variables. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Reading an oblique solution | Pattern coefficient (pattern matrix $\mathbf P$) | The coefficient of a factor in the simultaneous decomposition of a standardized indicator, read conditional on the other factors in the same representation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 |
| Reading an oblique solution | Structure correlation (structure matrix $\mathbf C=\mathbf P\boldsymbol\Phi$) | The zero-order indicator--factor correlation, which can be appreciable where the pattern coefficient is near zero because part of the relation travels through the factor correlation. Pattern and structure coincide only in an orthogonal solution. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 (defined as $\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$ in Chapter 1, Sec. 5) |
| Reading an oblique solution | Oblique communality as a quadratic form | $h_j^2=\mathbf p_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf p_j$, whose factor-correlation cross-products are part of the common variance. A row sum of squared pattern coefficients omits them and is a different quantity. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.2 |
| Residual evidence | Correlation residual matrix ($\mathbf E$) and off-diagonal RMS | Observed minus reproduced correlations, summarized by $\sqrt{2\sum_{j<k}e_{jk}^2/[p(p-1)]}$, which excludes variances. The largest absolute residual and the location of discrepancy carry information an average conceals, and this summary is not automatically any software statistic named RMSR or SRMR. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.1 |
| Residual evidence | Uniqueness boundary (bound-constrained uniqueness) | A fitted uniqueness at the implementation's lower bound rather than in the interior. It can signal too many factors, a redundant pair, sampling fluctuation or misspecification, and is different evidence from an interior estimate. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.3 |
| Preliminary summaries | KMO (Kaiser--Meyer--Olkin measure of sampling adequacy) | The ratio of summed squared zero-order correlations to that sum plus the summed squared partial correlations. It describes the input; it selects no factor count and is no minimum-sample-size calculation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2 |
| Preliminary summaries | Bartlett's test of sphericity | A normal-theory test of $H_0:\mathbf R_{\mathrm{population}}=\mathbf I$ on $p(p-1)/2$ df. Rejection says the indicators are not mutually uncorrelated, not that a low-dimensional factor model fits. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2 |
| Analytic sensitivity | Tucker's congruence coefficient | The cosine between two loading-column vectors, compared after column order and sign are aligned. It compares coefficient directions, not participant scores, and near-one congruence can hide an important difference for one item. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3 |
| Analytic sensitivity | Analytic sensitivity comparison | Changing one declared analytic choice at a time on the same records and comparing aligned solutions. It is same-sample evidence about analytic robustness, never an independent replication or a sampling interval. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3 |
| Analytic status | Frozen candidate specification | The exact item order, free and fixed relations, scaling, covariance and mean settings, estimation family and named rivals recorded before any confirmation evidence is inspected. Freezing is what makes a later comparison interpretable. | Chapter 2, Sec. 8 |
| Analytic status | Planned rival model | A restriction or broader alternative named before the confirmation outcome, distinguished from a post-hoc change, which changes analytic status and requires new evidence. | Chapter 2, Sec. 8 |

### Confirmatory Specification, Identification, and Estimation {#sec-p2-concepts-cfa .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Confirmatory specification | Confirmatory factor analysis (restricted factor model; CFA) | A common-factor model whose loading, residual, and factor-covariance entries are restricted before estimation, giving testable implications beyond the number of factors. The label describes restrictions and analytic history, not a favorable conclusion or a function name. | Chapter 3, Sec. 1 |
| Confirmatory specification | Exclusion restriction (fixed zero loading; absent arrow) | A loading entry set to zero as a substantive claim that the indicator has no direct relation to that factor. It does not state that the indicator and factor are uncorrelated, because correlated factors still induce a nonzero structure coefficient. | Chapter 3, Sec. 1 |
| Parameter status | Free, fixed, equality-constrained, bounded, and defined parameter | Estimated under the other restrictions; assigned a constant; required to share a value; restricted to a range; or computed from fitted parameters without adding freedom. A diagram shows which relations exist, not which status each has. | Chapter 3, Sec. 3 |
| Parameter status | Residual covariance (correlated residual; correlated uniqueness) | A freely estimated off-diagonal entry of $\boldsymbol\Theta$, occupying two symmetric cells and adding one free parameter. It changes one indicator pair's implied covariance, unlike a cross-loading, which changes a whole row and column. | Chapter 3, Sec. 3 |
| Latent metric | Marker scaling (reference indicator; unit loading identification) | Fixing one loading per factor at one, so the factor is expressed in that indicator's units and the factor variance is estimated. It does not set the factor variance to one and does not make the marker error-free. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Latent metric | Fixed-factor scaling (unit variance identification; `std.lv = TRUE`) | Fixing each factor variance at one and estimating every target loading, so a factor unit is one model standard deviation in a single-group model. It does not standardize the observed indicators. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Latent metric | Factor-scale reparameterization ($\mathbf D$ transformation) | The diagonal rescaling $\boldsymbol\Lambda^*=\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf D^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol\Phi^*=\mathbf D\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf D^{\mathsf T}$, which leaves the implied covariance and $\boldsymbol\Theta$ unchanged. Equivalence fails if a constraint is not transformed with the metric or a factor variance is on a boundary. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Observed units | Observed-unit rescaling ($\boldsymbol\Delta$ rescaling) | Replacing $\mathbf y$ by $\mathbf b+\boldsymbol\Delta\mathbf y$, which multiplies an indicator's intercept and loading by its factor, its variance and residual variance by that factor squared, and its covariance with an unchanged indicator by the factor. It changes the record, not the latent coordinates, and leaves fit unchanged under a consistently transformed model. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Observed units | Correlation reparameterization (standardized-indicator model) | Writing $\mathbf R=\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}$ with rescaled loading and residual matrices. It standardizes the indicators, not the factors, and its moment count differs from the covariance form because the unit diagonal is fixed. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Coefficient metrics | Latent-standardized and fully standardized loading (`std.lv`; `std.all`) | $\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}$ expresses a factor change in standard-deviation units in the indicator's raw unit; $\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}/\sqrt{\sigma_{jj}}$ standardizes both. A raw standard error is not the standardized coefficient's standard error, because the transformation uses estimated quantities. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Moment accounting | Observed moments, free parameters, and model degrees of freedom ($u$, $t$, $df=u-t$) | The distinct sample moments a declared representation supplies, the free coordinates the model estimates, and their difference. Necessary bookkeeping for one stated representation; neither identification nor quality, and unique covariance entries are not observations. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Moment accounting | Unrestricted-EFA dimension | The count of distinct covariance-model axes in an unrestricted $m$-factor solution, $pm+p-m(m-1)/2$ at regular full-rank points, which subtracts the continuous rotational freedom that changes the display without changing the reproduced covariance. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Identification (global, local, and generic; empirical or weak identification) | Whether the moments determine the parameters: uniquely over the admissible space, in a neighborhood, or except at exceptional values. Weak identification describes a recoverable model whose parameters are poorly distinguished, showing as unstable estimates and very large standard errors rather than an error message. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Two- and three-indicator sufficient conditions (connectedness) | A factor with at least three exclusive indicators is identified under a fixed scale and diagonal residuals; a factor with two exclusive indicators needs a nonzero covariance with another identified factor. Both are sufficient and neither is necessary, and the second depends on an estimated quantity. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Moment Jacobian rank check | Full column rank of $\partial\mathbf s/\partial\boldsymbol\vartheta^{\mathsf T}$ at a regular fitted point, a local diagnostic that supports local identification. It does not prove global uniqueness or uniform stability, and it is a check on the fitted solution rather than a structural proof. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Model relations | Nested, nonnested, and equivalent models (observational equivalence) | Nesting requires that every covariance matrix one model generates belongs to the other's set, shown by the restrictions producing the inclusion. Equal degrees of freedom imply neither nesting nor equivalence, and observational equivalence limits what covariance data can distinguish. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Estimation | Normal-theory ML discrepancy ($F_{\mathrm{ML}}$) | $\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)|+\operatorname{tr}\{\mathbf S\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)^{-1}\}-\log|\mathbf S|-p$, minimized over the admissible parameter space and normalized to zero at $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf S$. The covariance equation needs no normality; the conventional standard errors and test do. | Chapter 3, Sec. 7 (first used Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4) |
| Estimation | Covariance divisor convention ($\mathbf S_N$ against $\mathbf S_{N-1}$; normal against Wishart) | $\mathbf S_N=\{(N-1)/N\}\mathbf S_{N-1}$ is the normal-likelihood convention; the Wishart convention uses an $N-1$ covariance and multiplier. A supplied covariance matrix communicates neither the sample size nor the divisor, so the convention must be disclosed and never applied twice. | Chapter 3, Sec. 7 |
| Mean structure | Indicator intercepts and the latent location convention | Free indicator intercepts with latent intercepts fixed at zero add $p$ moments and $p$ parameters, leaving the covariance restrictions and degrees of freedom unchanged. Freeing both at once identifies no latent origin, because $\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf c$ with $\boldsymbol\nu-\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf c$ reproduces the same means. | Chapter 3, Sec. 5 |
| Solution quality | Convergence, admissibility, and the Heywood case | Convergence is an optimizer's stopping statement; admissibility requires positive residual variances and positive definite factor and implied covariance matrices. A negative or zero residual variance is a symptom of the whole decomposition and is neither a cosmetic warning nor something to replace by zero in a report. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Inference | Wald test of a linear restriction ($\mathbf R\boldsymbol\vartheta=\mathbf r$) | A $\chi^2_q$ test computed from the estimates and their covariance matrix, requiring the covariance between estimates and not only their variances. It tests the stated restriction conditional on the rest of the model; it is not a global-fit test and need not equal a refitted likelihood-ratio statistic. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Transition record | Evaluation transition record (handoff record) | What evaluation begins from: evidence identity, specification, parameter conventions, estimation settings, data handling, numerical status, parameter output, fitted moments, stored evaluation fields, and reproduction metadata. Storing those fields is not interpreting them. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Observed system | Parceling (item aggregation) | Fitting $\mathbf z=\mathbf A\mathbf y$ with $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf z)=\mathbf A\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}$. Reducing dimension lets different item-level patterns give the same parcel covariance, so a well-fitting parcel model does not establish the item-level restrictions. | Chapter 3, Appendix |

### Evaluation, Comparison, Reliability, and Extensions {#sec-p2-concepts-evaluation .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Global fit | Model chi-square (exact-fit test; likelihood-ratio model test) | $T_M=N\widehat F_{\mathrm{ML}}$ referred to $\chi^2_{df_M}$, testing whether some admissible parameter vector reproduces the population moment structure exactly. Nonrejection is not acceptance of the model, and rejection at large $N$ is evidence against exact fit rather than a measure of its magnitude. | Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | RMSEA (root mean square error of approximation) with its 90% interval | Estimated discrepancy per degree of freedom, $\sqrt{\max\{(T_M-df_M)/(N\,df_M),0\}}$, comparable across models of different size, with an interval obtained by inverting a noncentral chi-square reference. A zero estimate is a truncation, not zero residuals; the convention ($N$ or $N-1$) must be named. | Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | Incremental fit index (CFI; TLI or NNFI) with its independence baseline | Improvement of the model relative to a stated reference rather than relative to exact fit. The usual baseline frees the observed variances and fixes all covariances to zero, so a high value depends on how poor that baseline is; TLI is not bounded by one. | Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | SRMR (standardized root mean square residual) | Root mean square of observed-SD-standardized covariance residuals over one triangle including the diagonal. Not a mean absolute residual; a small value can hide a few large cells among many near-zero ones. | Chapter 4, Sec. 3 |
| Local diagnosis | Covariance residual (raw; observed-SD-standardized; correlation residual) | Observed minus implied covariance, either in the product of the two indicators' units, divided by the product of observed SDs, or as a difference of separately formed correlations. None is a residual divided by its sampling standard error, so none is automatically a $z$ statistic. | Chapter 4, Sec. 3 |
| Local diagnosis | Modification index (score statistic; Lagrange multiplier) and expected parameter change (EPC; standardized EPC) | A local one-parameter approximation to the improvement from releasing one fixed restriction, with the approximate value the released parameter would take. Read with the residual pattern, the parameter's meaning, and the status of the search; not the exact LR change, and not an instruction. | Chapter 4, Sec. 6 |
| Comparison | Nested difference test ($\chi^2$ difference; likelihood-ratio difference test) | $\Delta T=T_R-T_U$ on $\Delta df=df_R-df_U$ for regularly nested, compatible ML fits on identical cases, outcomes, scale, mean structure, and likelihood convention. A smaller parameter count is not proof of nesting, and failure to reject is not equivalence. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Information criteria for covariance structures (AIC; BIC) eligibility | $-2\ell+2q$ and $-2\ell+q\log N$ with $q$ the effective free-parameter count. They rank eligible candidates fitted to the same observations and outcomes under one likelihood convention, including nonnested ones; neither is a test or an adequacy index. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Score, Wald, and likelihood-ratio views of one restriction | Three statistics for one null: slope and information at the restricted fit; distance of the unrestricted estimate from the restriction relative to its uncertainty; difference of optimized likelihoods. Asymptotic equivalence is not finite-sample equality. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Equivalent models (covariance-equivalent representation) | Distinct specifications that imply the same fitted covariance matrix, and hence the same statistic, df, and every fit index. No amount of covariance data can choose between them; only theory and evidence beyond reproduced covariance can. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Higher-order factor model (second-order factor; first-order disturbance) | A model in which one further latent variable accounts for the covariances among first-order factors, $\boldsymbol\Phi_l=\boldsymbol\gamma\boldsymbol\gamma^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Psi_h$. The first-order disturbances are not indicator residuals, and the form imposes $m(m-3)/2$ restrictions, hence none when $m=3$. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Bifactor model (general plus orthogonal specific or group factors) | Every item loads directly on one general factor and one assigned specific factor, all factors mutually orthogonal. A specific factor is common variance among its items after the general factor is held constant, not an item residual, and the model is generally nonnested against a correlated-factor model of the same items. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Schmid-Leiman transformation and the proportionality restriction | The algebraic rewriting of a higher-order model as an orthogonal general factor with loadings $\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\gamma$ and specific factors with loadings $\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\Psi_h^{1/2}$. Because both come from one loading matrix, each simple-structure item in a domain splits its common variance in the ratio $\gamma_k/\psi_{h,k}^{1/2}$; a freely estimated bifactor model is not bound by that ratio. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Method effect; testlet effect | Common variance among items sharing a format (reverse keying, response scale, informant) or a stimulus (passage, vignette, apparatus). Both are design-known groupings and the least controversial motivation for a specific factor, which generalizes a freed residual covariance to several items. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Reliability | Model-based omega for a declared score, $\omega(\mathbf w)$ (composite reliability) | The proportion of a declared weighted composite's model-implied variance attributable to all modeled common factors. It retains cross-loadings, factor correlations, and modeled residual covariances, and is conditional on model, weights, and sample. | Chapter 4, Sec. 8 |
| Reliability | Omega-hierarchical, $\omega_h(\mathbf w)$ | The share of a declared score's variance attributable specifically to a bifactor general factor. Its complement within total omega is modeled reliable specific-factor variance, not error, and a substantial value does not establish essential unidimensionality. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Reliability | Average variance extracted (AVE) and coefficient $H$ as bounded neighbours | AVE summarizes average communality for a simple fully-standardized single-factor item set; $H=a/(1+a)$ with $a=\boldsymbol\lambda^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Theta^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda$ is a maximum over optimally weighted composites. Neither is the reliability of a stated unit-weighted score, and neither applies unqualified to a cross-loading subscale. | Chapter 4, Appendix |
| Scores | Factor score (regression or conditional-mean score; Bartlett score) and factor-score determinacy | A model-dependent linear prediction of a latent variable from the indicators, whose weights use the whole fitted structure; determinacy is the model-based correlation between factor and prediction. A score is a prediction with nonzero conditional variance, not an observed latent value. | Chapter 4, Sec. 8 |
| Analytic history | Pseudo-true (population-ML) parameter and population discrepancy ($F_0$; population RMSEA) | The optimum of a misspecified model fitted to the exact generating covariance, and the discrepancy remaining there. Displacement at this optimum is deterministic under two stated specifications, not sampling fluctuation and not finite-sample estimator bias. | Chapter 4, Sec. 7 |
| Analytic history | Post-selection revision and independent revalidation | A change suggested by inspecting a body of evidence is exploratory with respect to that evidence, whatever function fits it; only records not used to suggest it can support it, and a retest that fails to support it does not prove the parameter is zero. | Chapter 4, Sec. 6 |
